optionDescriptions.downBeforeRedeploy: Run docker compose down before the redeploy bring-up step.
optionDescriptions.pullBeforeRedeploy: Pull the latest images before reusing the saved compose project definition.
optionDescriptions.buildBeforeUp: Add --build to docker compose up when the redeploy flow reaches bring-up.
optionDescriptions.forceRecreate: Add --force-recreate so all containers are recreated during bring-up.
optionDescriptions.removeOrphans: Add --remove-orphans so docker compose up removes orphaned containers no longer declared by this project.
optionDescriptions.waitAfterUp: Add --wait so compose up blocks until declared services report ready.
optionDescriptions.waitTimeoutSeconds: Only applies when Wait After Up is enabled. Accepted range: 1 to 3600 seconds.
optionDescriptions.renewAnonVolumes: Add --renew-anon-volumes so docker compose up does not reuse anonymous volumes from older containers.
optionDescriptions.pruneImagesAfterRedeploy: Run docker image prune -f after redeploy completes.

downBeforeRedeploy.tooltip: Stop and remove the current Compose resources before the new up runs. This creates a clear downtime window but resets stale container and network state.
downBeforeRedeploy.effect: Changes redeploy into a two-step flow: run docker compose down first, then run a fresh docker compose up.
downBeforeRedeploy.scenarios: Use it when you need a clean restart or suspect stale containers, networks, or mounts are contaminating the current deployment.
downBeforeRedeploy.risks: This creates an explicit downtime window. Services are unavailable between down and up, and project-scoped resources are removed before startup resumes.
downBeforeRedeploy.recommendation: Enable it only when you accept the downtime window and need a full reset instead of an in-place bring-up.

pullBeforeRedeploy.tooltip: Pull images before reusing the current Compose definition. Best when image tags are updated continuously.
pullBeforeRedeploy.effect: Runs docker compose pull before the bring-up phase so the project refreshes its referenced images first.
pullBeforeRedeploy.scenarios: Use it when CI regularly pushes images, when tags like latest are reused, or when redeploy should always prefer the newest remote image.
pullBeforeRedeploy.risks: It adds network time and can pull in an unexpected new image version, which may change behavior or make rollback slower.
pullBeforeRedeploy.recommendation: Keep it off for pinned immutable tags. Consider enabling it when the deployment flow depends on remote image updates.

buildBeforeUp.tooltip: Add --build to up so local images are rebuilt first. Best for projects driven by local Dockerfiles or changed source code.
buildBeforeUp.effect: Adds --build to docker compose up so redeploy rebuilds the local image before starting containers.
buildBeforeUp.scenarios: Use it when Dockerfiles, build contexts, dependencies, or application source changed and the project relies on local image builds.
buildBeforeUp.risks: It increases deployment time, especially when caches are cold. Build failures also block the redeploy entirely.
buildBeforeUp.recommendation: Leave it off unless rebuilding locally is part of the normal deployment path for this project.

forceRecreate.tooltip: Add --force-recreate so containers are rebuilt even if Compose sees no config diff. Useful for flushing bad state, but noisier than a normal up.
forceRecreate.effect: Adds --force-recreate to docker compose up so all service containers are recreated during bring-up.
forceRecreate.scenarios: Use it when you suspect container state drift, need mounts or environment changes to be reapplied aggressively, or a plain restart is not enough.
forceRecreate.risks: It causes more restarts and more churn than a normal up. Services with warm caches or local state will feel the reset more strongly.
forceRecreate.recommendation: Leave it off by default and enable it only when you intentionally want a forced container refresh.

removeOrphans.tooltip: Add --remove-orphans so old containers not defined in the current Compose files are cleaned up automatically. Useful after renames, splits, or removals.
removeOrphans.effect: Adds --remove-orphans to docker compose up so containers that no longer exist in the current Compose definition are removed automatically.
removeOrphans.scenarios: Use it after service renames, module splits, service removals, or whenever historical containers should be cleaned up as part of redeploy.
removeOrphans.risks: It removes leftover containers in the same Compose project scope. If you still rely on one of those undeclared containers, it will be removed as well.
removeOrphans.recommendation: Recommended. It keeps long-lived Compose projects from accumulating confusing leftovers.

waitAfterUp.tooltip: Add --wait after up. With healthchecks, Compose waits for healthy; without healthchecks, it usually only knows whether containers are running.
waitAfterUp.effect: Turns startup into a synchronous readiness wait so Graft does not finish the action until Compose reports services as ready.
waitAfterUp.scenarios: Use it when operators need a stronger readiness signal before considering the redeploy complete or before running follow-up actions.
waitAfterUp.risks: It increases feedback time. Without service healthchecks, the readiness signal is weaker and may only mean the container reached running state.
waitAfterUp.recommendation: Use it when readiness matters, and prefer adding healthchecks first so the wait result is meaningful.

waitTimeoutSeconds.tooltip: Limit how long --wait can block. Too short causes false failures; too long slows deployment feedback.
waitTimeoutSeconds.effect: Controls the maximum duration for docker compose up -d --wait before the wait is treated as timed out.
waitTimeoutSeconds.scenarios: Use it for slow-start services, first-run migrations, cold caches, or environments whose startup time varies noticeably.
waitTimeoutSeconds.risks: A timeout that is too small can mark healthy-but-slow startups as failures. A timeout that is too large slows release and debugging feedback loops.
waitTimeoutSeconds.recommendation: Tune it per environment based on observed startup time, with enough buffer for normal variance.

renewAnonVolumes.tooltip: Add --renew-anon-volumes so old anonymous volumes are not reused. Old data in anonymous volumes may no longer be reused by new containers.
renewAnonVolumes.effect: Adds --renew-anon-volumes to docker compose up so recreated containers get fresh anonymous volumes instead of reusing the previous ones.
renewAnonVolumes.scenarios: Use it when you intentionally want to clear anonymous cache/state or suspect the old anonymous volume data is corrupted.
renewAnonVolumes.risks: Old data in anonymous volumes may no longer be reused by the new containers, which can wipe caches, transient state, or misplaced application data.
renewAnonVolumes.recommendation: Treat this as dangerous. Enable it only when you know what lives in the anonymous volumes and accept losing reuse of the old data.

pruneImagesAfterRedeploy.tooltip: Run docker image prune -f after redeploy. This is a Docker host-level cleanup, not something scoped only to the current Compose project.
pruneImagesAfterRedeploy.effect: Runs docker image prune -f after redeploy so unused images on the Docker host are cleaned up automatically.
pruneImagesAfterRedeploy.scenarios: Use it on tightly managed hosts with disk pressure and frequent image churn, especially when automatic image cleanup is already an accepted policy.
pruneImagesAfterRedeploy.risks: This is a Docker host-level action, not one limited to the current Compose project. It can affect image cache, rollback speed, or later build performance for other workloads on the same host.
pruneImagesAfterRedeploy.recommendation: Leave it off unless the host is intentionally managed that way and reclaiming image space is worth the wider side effects.
